Article:

The European Commission announced on Tuesday that it would delay parts of its digital rulebook by twelve months, citing industry readiness concerns. The delay affects transparency obligations originally due in August.

Answer:

The European Commission announced the delay because they cited industry readiness concerns. It affects transparency obligations originally due in August.

Supporting detail from the news article:

"The European Commission has delayed parts of its digital rulebook by 12 months, citing industry readiness concerns."

"Under the original plan, the rules were supposed to be implemented in August."
comparisons.base:
Based on the information provided, the European Commission delayed parts of its digital rulebook by twelve months. This decision was made with the intention of addressing industry readiness concerns. 

The delay specifically affects transparency obligations that were initially scheduled for implementation in August. These obligations were part of the broader digital rulebook designed to regulate various aspects of digital markets within the EU. By pushing back these requirements, the commission aims to give industries more time to prepare and adapt to the regulations, ensuring they are ready before enforcement begins.

Regulators in three countries have launched a joint investigation into a facial recognition company that they say illegally collected images of people without their permission, according to media reports.

The companies involved include the U.S.-based Clearview AI, which has been accused of scraping millions of photos from social media sites; the Chinese tech giant Baidu; and the French firm DeepSDK, which was acquired by Baidu last year.

"The allegations made against us are false," the company added.

Baidu did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

DeepSDK also denied wrongdoing, saying it had "no knowledge of any illegal activity." It added that it would work with authorities as part of the investigation.

In a separate development, China's National Supervisory Commission announced Thursday that it had launched an investigation into the use of facial recognition technology at public events, including sports games and concerts.

The commission said it would investigate whether such uses were legal and if there was evidence of abuse.

China has become one of the world's largest users of facial recognition technology, with hundreds of cities using the system to monitor citizens' movements and activities.

Facial recognition systems can be trained to identify individuals even when they're wearing masks or other coverings, raising concerns among privacy advocates who worry that governments could use them to track people's movements and behavior.

A number of countries have recently introduced new laws regulating the use of facial recognition technology, including France, Germany, Italy, Spain, and the United Kingdom.

In July, the European Union approved a draft law that would ban the use of biometric data -- including facial recognition -- unless it is necessary for national security or public safety reasons.

However, some experts warn that the proposed EU legislation may still allow for widespread use of facial recognition technology, particularly in cases where it is used to combat crime.
